body_markdown:
This is the car that haunted my childhood. Its athletic proportions, draped in vibrant Rangoon Red paint; those honed edges—even the terraced, hexagonal-pyramid wheel covers were unforgettable to a six-year-old already steeped in the car culture of my native Southern California.


On a trip to my grandparents’ home in Northern California, there it was: My uncle and soon-to-be aunt had come to visit as well, and I’ve never forgotten the image of the Mustang they’d driven over, parked at the curb next to the steep sidewalk on the precipice of Terrace Drive in Millbrae, just south of San Francisco. The wheels were dutifully curbed to the front, as every resident and visitor was trained to do.


Appropriately fascinated, I still remember asking to go out to the sidewalk and look at it. Despite the fact that Ford’s formal proposal for the car was modestly named the[“Special Falcon Program,”](https://www.hagerty.com/media/design/why-the-1965-mustangs-design-will-never-go-out-of-style/) the 1965 Mustang was undeniably one of the most significant automotive designs in American automotive history. At my age, no way was I aware of that. I do believe, though, that I recognized the car as something special.


Aunt Karen, circa 1965.


Eric Evarts


My Aunt Karen, after spending a few years in a Jaguar XK150 coupe during a previous marriage, had ordered her Mustang—a C-code coupe—new in September of 1964, through a program offered by the departing husband’s employer. Its only options: the 289-cubic-inch V-8, a three-speed automatic transmission, power steering and an AM radio. A famous labor strike delayed production of Ford’s red-hot, Falcon-in-a-tux pony car until January of 1965, when she took delivery. My Uncle Don, then getting started in business after two tours of duty in Vietnam, brought the car into the family when he married Karen a year after I first laid eyes on it.


Now, after 61 years of logging every oil change, of keeping a dedicated space for it in their garage no matter what daily life required, and after faithfully pulling the car out for at least a run to the grocery store every two weeks throughout those six-plus decades, she decided it’s time to sell.


Why did she keep it all these years? “It just might be because your uncle wanted me to sell it!” she retorts, during an appearance by her ornery side. As the family’s resident car guy, I’d been recruited to help. It wasn’t an easy decision for either of us.


Eric Evarts


Eric Evarts


Eric Evarts


Eric Evarts


I didn’t see Karen or the Mustang for several years after that initial visit. Busy parents; busy lives; long distances, California traffic. All of that.


A few months later, my family took our first long road trip out of state, to Colorado, for a week at a summer camp I’d eventually attend. To keep my little brother and me entertained over three days in the back seat of the family Dodge Polara, my parents bought us each three Matchbox cars of our choice. I picked a pair of Ford F-150s (one carrying dogs and the other a tiger), plus a ’65 Mustang with real steering, operated by a slider switch below the driver’s door. It was a white fastback.


Five or six years later, we visited Uncle Don and Aunt Karen several times after they moved to Newport Beach, just south of Los Angeles. They bought a bungalow on Balboa Peninsula and expanded it as kids arrived, with several bedrooms over the garage in the alley. The Mustang was always carefully tucked away in that garage, even during construction. I found excuses to go look at it—taking out the trash, fetching a broom—and was a bit chagrined to recall that it was just a coupe, not a fastback. And with an automatic, not a manual. On the flip side, it never looked any less sharp or polished than that first time its sparkling red enamel drew me in.


As a faithful reader of the Los Angeles-based *Road & Track, Motor Trend* and *Hot Rod* magazines, my tastes trended toward imported iron: Porsches, Volkswagens, and even Hondas. But I always maintained a soft spot for the Mustang.


During the school board campaign era.


Eric Evarts


Don and Karen came to visit us after we moved to Northern California when I was in high school, showing up in the first of a string of family-friendly Chevrolet G10 conversion vans. Don commuted to work in a company-owned Mercedes W126 300SD, driven slowly and cautiously, for 20 years. The Mustang typically sat beside it in the garage, rolled out mostly for bi-weekly grocery runs and occasional soccer pickups.


In 1990, after a challenging experience teaching social studies to inner-city Los Angeles teens, Karen twice ran for a spot on the school board, both times unsuccessfully. Apparently a dissenter, spotting her signature red Mustang parked on the street, keyed a profane message into the rear roof pillar. The vandal was spell-challenged: One of the words the body shop tried to buff out was the word “Looser,” along with a swoop on the passenger door. Faint curls remain visible, though they don’t really show in photos.


The Mustang got a new short block in 1976 after the engine began smoking. The Ford 8-inch rear end has wept a bit for years, but her mechanic said it wasn’t worth fixing. In the 1980s, Karen replaced the AM radio with an AM/FM cassette deck, which involved cutting the original dash to fit. (It was later restored.)


Several years ago, Karen discovered the joys of taking her Mustang to local car shows. She has come to appreciate what, for her, is a refreshed perspective on life in general, cars in particular.


Sharing the car love with future generations.


Eric Evarts


For years, her family expanded with kids and grandkids, but Karen was reluctant to part with the Mustang, I think in part because too many family members were interested in it, and she didn’t want to disappoint anyone. But my high-achieving, career-focused cousins and their spouses evidently concluded that the Mustang is at best a distraction, at worst, may even be dangerous, given its lack of modern safety equipment.


Recently, she has spoken to me about selling the Mustang, sometimes asking for advice on repairs: The starter (repeatedly), the alternator, the carburetor; a “289” badge that fell off the right front fender. Finally, in a conversation we had following her and Don’s 50th wedding anniversary party, she made the decision: She wanted to hold onto the car just long enough for her first-born grandson, Duncan—her only remaining heir with a genuine interest in cars—to drive it once he turned 16 and got his license.


He flew down to drive the Mustang in July. “So much fun!” she said, after introducing him to the ’65. Don taught him to check the oil and other fluids before starting out, and Karen taught him the ancient art of cold starting an American V-8 with an Autolite carburetor. Photos you see here show Duncan behind the wheel wearing a big grin, despite adult supervision.


Despite decades spent admiring Karen’s car, and 20 years of testing 2000-odd new vehicles due to my auto-writing career, I’d never driven her Mustang. Finally, that was about to change.


Duncan and Karen.


Eric Evarts


Duncan behind the wheel.


Eric Evarts


I traveled to Newport Beach to help Karen and the Mustang prepare for the upcoming online auction, including taking a plethora of the required photos. First, grandson Duncan would drive the car, then I’d have my chance.


Initially, the Mustang declined to cooperate. With Don at the wheel, I opened the hood and began shooting a cold-start video. I looked through the viewfinder to see a waterfall of gasoline pouring from the carburetor onto the intake manifold. “Shut it down!” I yelled, waving my free arm. We’d planned to take the Mustang to Karen’s mechanic anyway, in part to put it up on the lift to snap some photos from underneath, and that expanded into getting the carb resealed.


We shot the Mustang at a handy, scenic waterfront location, and when we decided to take the car to dinner in town that night, my decades-delayed turn to drive it finally arrived. Don graciously folded himself into the back seat (thus torquing his back for the remainder of the evening), and we headed off.


Eric Evarts


I’d driven a comparable Mustang with the inline six-cylinder, but promptly learned that even this base 289 V-8, rated at 200 horsepower, genuinely transforms the car. It still felt light on its hooves, but planted on the road in a way that the straight-six sample just didn’t. Karen had prepared me for the absence of power brakes; unlike the pedal on my old VW Beetle, this one took some actual effort, as well as some prior planning, to stop the car. These days, Karen uses both feet.


With the Mustang’s standard bucket seats, it makes for a tight cockpit. The thin, wide-around steering wheel sits right in your face, all the better for cranking it against the weight of the V-8 when the car is barely moving.


Underway, though, the steering feels direct off-center, if a tad slow. But 80,000 miles of wear on the bushings and gear requires an elbows-up, Muppet-like driving imitation to maintain a straight line down the road.


Eric Evarts


On the way home, traffic lightened, and after years of wondering what the car could do, I took advantage of a straight stretch of pavement as an opportunity to press my elders into their seatbacks. Even without the optional four-barrel carb or the GT package, and with the stock 2.80 rear-end, it scoots along with surprising authority.


After that, I tried all the accessories. It’s amazing to find a car this old with the glove box latch, cigarette lighter and footwell courtesy lamps still working, as were the high beams and the foot-button switch that operates them.


Recalling that Karen had long complained about difficulty with cold starts, I asked her about the unlabeled black knob to the left of the steering column. I assumed it was the manual choke, but she said she’d never used it.


The next morning, I planned to demonstrate how the choke worked. I pulled it out a little, but when I turned the key—nothing but a click. I imagine that Karen must have thought it was a faulty choke, but she didn’t suggest it out loud.


We hooked jumper cables up to my daughter’s Hyundai that I had borrowed for the final leg of my trip, pleased that she still had the emergency kit in the trunk that I’d bought her for Christmas three years earlier. As before, nothing but a click.


Eric Evarts


An hour later, AAA showed up for one of its all-too-regular recent visits with the Mustang. Jamie, the driver, was confident it wasn’t the battery but the starter; as he progressed through school, he had helped his father restore more than a dozen pony cars, including some Mustangs. He gamely confirmed his diagnosis when the Mustang continued its click-only performance. Several hours later, it was off to the shop aboard a flatbed.


That meant our photo sessions were over. This was Saturday morning. It would be Monday until the Mustang was repaired, and I had a red-eye flight back to New York on Sunday night.


Oh, well. By long distance, I’d get a full inspection report and added it to the auction package, but while I was there the rest of that weekend, we simply caught up. Karen and Don and I assembled a timeline of the Mustang’s life—and ours, for that matter—from memory, helped along by Karen’s maintenance logs. Don dug out the family Bible; my daughter came to visit for dinner and showed off her new engagement ring; Don told me some stories from the Vietnam War, which he rarely shares. I wore my family out with questions.


Eric Evarts


I’m not really sorry not to be there for the auction, since I am the “official” seller and am managing virtually all aspects of the no-reserve auction, which continues through Monday on one of the big auction sites. You can check its progress by clicking here, which[links to a modest website](https://sites.google.com/view/auntkarensmustang/home) I built for the Mustang.


So many memories, and hopefully, many more to come. Just not with my family.


We’ll miss it.


Eric Evarts


The post[Farewell, Family Heirloom: One-Owner 1965 Mustang Ready for a New Home](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/farewell-family-heirloom-one-owner-1965-mustang-ready-for-a-new-home/) appeared first on[Hagerty Media](https://www.hagerty.com/media) .
